analysis.one_liner: Lets any small business opt out of nearly every federal regulation issued since 2009.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a cosponsor and died in the House Small Business Committee at the end of the 114th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any 'small business' — a category covering most American firms — simply notify a federal agency and stop following any federal rule issued on or after January 20, 2009. That sweeps in consumer product safety rules, food safety standards, workplace safety rules, wage and overtime protections, environmental limits, and financial rules. The only string attached is that the business must label affected products as no longer subject to the rule, and it cannot opt out of Defense or Homeland Security rules that agency heads deem necessary for national security [S2][S3]. It was referred to the House Small Business Committee and never moved again [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Small business owners who would save the cost of complying with consumer, safety, labor, and environmental rules — gaining an advantage over larger competitors who must still follow them.

how_it_helps.text: Any small business could elect, by written notice, to be exempt from any federal rule issued on or after January 20, 2009, with the exemption effective 30 days later [S2][S3].
The bill does not limit which rules can be ignored, so it reaches consumer product safety, food, workplace, wage, environmental, and financial regulations alike [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, workers, and the public, who lose the protection of those rules whenever they buy from, work for, or live near an exempt business. Compliant larger competitors also lose out to firms that can undercut them by skipping the rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill's only protection for the public is a label: an exempt business must mark products as 'no longer subject to' the rule, which tells a shopper a product is unregulated but does not make it safe [S3].

An exempt business that violates the labeling notice is penalized only for skipping the label — not for the underlying harm to a consumer or worker — so the penalty structure targets paperwork rather than dangerous products [S3].

Because the Small Business Act definition of 'small business concern' covers the vast majority of American firms, the bill would open a wide hole in federal regulation, and businesses that follow the rules would be undercut by those that opt out [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — lower compliance costs for small firms — is real but comes entirely from shifting risk onto customers, employees, and neighbors. The public-notice labeling is a thin substitute for the actual rules: a warning that a product is unregulated is not protection. The bill offers nothing to the people on the other side of the transaction.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Small Business Committee on January 6, 2015, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so the bill died when the 114th Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Representative Scott Garrett introduced the bill on January 6, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Small Business [S1][S5].
No further action was taken after the referral, and the bill received no committee vote and no floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and workers keep the existing rules of the road. Compliant businesses also benefit, since no competitor gains the right to skip the rules they must follow.

for.name: Rep. Scott Garrett
for.role: Sponsor, House Small Business Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Small Business Committee.

against.name: House Committee on Small Business
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill attracted no cosponsors from either party [S4], and no vote was ever recorded, so there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would let small firms stop following consumer, safety, labor, and environmental rules issued since 2009, cutting their costs by shifting risk onto customers and workers. The opt-out only requires a label saying the product is no longer subject to the rule [S2][S3].

Businesses too large to qualify, or that chose to keep following the rules, would compete against exempt rivals whose savings would let them undercut on price. Their interest here runs with the public's in keeping rules uniform.
